> Study Air Station is a desk air-quality monitor for students. Stuffy, polluted air makes it hard to focus, and you usually can’t tell until you feel tired or get a headache. This device measures the air around you and tells you when to act.

## Design

### 2026-11-08: I spent this session on the schematic in KiCad, starting from the Schematik desk air quality monitor as a reference. I kept the idea and redrew everything with my own pin choices.

**4h**

I spent this session on the schematic in KiCad, starting from the Schematik desk air quality monitor as a reference. I kept the idea and redrew everything with my own pin choices.

Power comes in on a screw terminal and passes through a 1N5819 diode against reverse polarity, then onto the 5 V rail. A 470 uF capacitor sits on the 5 V rail and 100 nF capacitors on 5 V and 3.3 V.

The fan is switched on the ground side by an IRLZ44N. A 100 ohm resistor sits in series with the gate and a 10k resistor pulls the gate down so the fan stays off while the ESP32 boots. A second 1N5819 across the fan absorbs the spike when it turns off.

I spent the most time on the ESP32 pins. The two buttons and the SD card MISO line use the input-only pins IO36, IO39 and IO34. Those pins have no internal pull-ups, so each button gets an external 10k pull-up. I left IO12 unused because it is a boot strapping pin. The display and the SD card share SCK and MOSI and have their own chip selects. The SCD40 uses I2C on IO21 and IO22, and the PMS5003 uses UART2 on IO16 and IO17.

I ran the electrical rules check and fixed the wires that were off the schematic grid. It now reports 0 violations. Next I’ll lay out the PCB.

### 2026-11-08: I laid out the PCB for the air station in KiCad. The board is 100 x 80 mm, two layers, with a ground pour on both sides.

**3h**

I laid out the PCB for the air station in KiCad. The board is 100 x 80 mm, two layers, with a ground pour on both sides.

I started with placement. The ESP32 sockets go in the middle. The display, SD module, SCD40 and PMS5003 headers sit close to the ESP32 pins they connect to, so the display lines run straight up to the header without crossing. The power input, diode and bulk capacitor are bottom left. The fan terminal, MOSFET and flyback diode are bottom right.

Then I routed the board. I made the 5 V trace 0.8 mm and the fan trace 0.6 mm because they carry the most current, and kept signals at 0.25 mm. I added stitching vias to join the two ground pours and keep copper islands from floating. I put pin names on the silkscreen next to every header and fixed labels that overlapped pads.

I ran the design rule check against the schematic and fixed everything it flagged until it reported 0 violations and 0 unconnected pads.

### 2026-11-08: Designed the enclosure from scratch in CadQuery as a two-part case: a base that holds the PCB and a flat lid with a TFT window and two button caps. I modeled every module as a keep-out box on the boar

**2h**

Designed the enclosure from scratch in CadQuery as a two-part case: a base that holds the PCB and a flat lid with a TFT window and two button caps. I modeled every module as a keep-out box on the board (ESP32 socket, TFT, SCD40 and microSD on cable headers, PMS5003, fan, buzzer, LED) and sized the case around them. The result is 160 x 86 x 32.4 mm. I cut the USB port opening, the fan opening with four screw holes, and vent slots for airflow to the sensors. I then ran an interference check between the parts. It caught the TFT module clashing with the lid lip, which I fixed by shifting the display 1.5 mm, and a gap under the button caps, which I fixed by lengthening the posts to 8.1 mm. The final check shows 0 clashes. Exported the assembly as an editable STEP file.

### 2026-11-08: Wrote the full firmware for the ESP32 as one Arduino sketch. I wrote a raw I2C driver for the SCD40 (stop, set offset and altitude, start, ready check, read) with the Sensirion CRC8 check, and a PMS50

**4h**

Wrote the full firmware for the ESP32 as one Arduino sketch. I wrote a raw I2C driver for the SCD40 (stop, set offset and altitude, start, ready check, read) with the Sensirion CRC8 check, and a PMS5003 frame parser that reads the 32-byte UART frame, checks the sum and resyncs after stray bytes. Air quality is classified with hysteresis, so a state is entered at the threshold and left at 90 percent of it. The fan switches on at 1000 ppm CO2 or 25 ug/m3 PM2.5 with a 60 s minimum dwell, and the buzzer beeps every 30 s in alert. The silence button mutes it for 10 minutes, the page button changes the display screen, and a long press changes the fan mode. The TFT shows the live readings and a 24 hour history graph. I added a minute-by-minute CSV log on the microSD card, NTP time, Telegram alerts with a repeat and a recovery message, and a password-protected web dashboard. Thresholds and fan mode are stored in flash, so they survive a reboot. Compiled it in Arduino IDE for the ESP32 Dev Module: 88 percent of program storage and 15 percent of RAM. Fixed one build error where the button struct had to be declared before the functions that use it.

### 2026-11-08: Set up a full simulation of the Study Air Station in Wokwi so the firmware could run before the hardware is built. I wired the ESP32 DevKit to a TFT, microSD card, buzzer, RGB LED, a fan indicator LED

**4h**

Set up a full simulation of the Study Air Station in Wokwi so the firmware could run before the hardware is built. I wired the ESP32 DevKit to a TFT, microSD card, buzzer, RGB LED, a fan indicator LED on the MOSFET gate pin, and the silence and page buttons with 10k pull-ups, using the same GPIO pins as the schematic. Wokwi has no SCD40, PMS5003 or ST7789, so I made a simulation copy of the sketch. It swaps in an ILI9341 display and replaces the two sensor drivers with generated CO2, temperature, humidity and particle values that cycle through the warn and alert ranges. Everything else is the real firmware code. I fixed a build failure caused by the original ST7789 library, and corrected the display orientation by rotating the part. I then ran it and watched the live readings, the status bar, the history chart, the LED colour changes, the fan indicator switching on at the threshold, and the page button changing screens.
